name: Low-pressure liquid propellant tank
unit: kg of tank per litre of propellant
notes: The base figure every non-pressurised storage class in PROPELLANTS_REFERENCE multiplies.  Bracketed by three flight articles: Shuttle ET 0.0129 kg/L (big dumb tank, cheap per litre), Falcon 9 stage 2 ~0.033, Centaur III ~0.035 (the last two include thrust structure and avionics mounts).  Derivation and the ∝V-vs-∝V^⅔ caveat are at _TANK_BASE_KG_PER_L.

name: COPV burst performance factor
unit: J per kg (PV/W)
notes:
~40 km × g0.  Sets tank mass for every supercritical-gas propellant: m/V = 1.5·p_operating/(PV/W).  This is why xenon at 10 MPa pays 1.9% of its mass in tankage and krypton at 18 MPa pays 12.5% — the cheaper propellant needs the heavier bottle, and the trade did not exist in this model before.
Comparator: six cryogenic NASA test articles on two liner configurations burst at P_b·V/W of 326.5-416.6 kJ/kg (NTRS 20080009730, Tables 1-3), bracketing this value, for small 1.8 ft3 helium-pressurant vessels with minimum burst at 1.5x MOP; the range here stays an estimate for other sizes and materials (General_Research rc-417).  NASA's other COPV reports (Greene et al., NTRS 20100021151; Kezirian, Johnson & Phoenix, NTRS 20110015972; Parker & Prosser, NASA/TM-20260002192) cover stress rupture and flight rationale, not a performance factor.

name: Multi-layer insulation (passive)
unit: kg per m² of tank surface
notes:
60-layer aluminised-Mylar blanket, the passive baseline behind every boiloff_pct_per_day figure in the propellant table. Carried inside the storage-class tank multipliers rather than as a separate area term, because this pipeline never computes a tank's surface area — only its volume.
ESTIMATE: neither the 60 layers nor the 1.2 kg/m² has a source.  NASA's boil-off reduction tests (Plachta, Johnson & Feller, NTRS 20150000134) used 30-layer, 18-layer and 75-layer blankets and give no areal density.  Comparator: NASA KSC cryogenic MLI tests measured 2.98 kg/m2 for a 60-layer blanket and 2.41 for a 40-layer one (Johnson, NTRS 20110014002, Table 3), test coupons with seams; the 1.2 estimate stays under review (General_Research rc-320).

name: Zero-boil-off cryocooler (20 K)
unit: W electrical input per W lifted at 20 K
notes:
Reverse-turbo-Brayton.  NASA's 20 W / 20 K unit measured 91.6 W/W at its 285 K-reject test point, 14.5% of Carnot (best point 15.6%), against a programme threshold of 80 W/W, which is this row, and a goal of 60 (Nugent, Grotenrath & Johnson 2022, NTRS 20220009350, Tables 1 and 3).  The Gifford-McMahon cooler on the MHTB zero-boil-off test needed 350 W/W, 4% of Carnot (Hastings et al., NASA/TP-2010-216453).  Carnot at 20 K against a 300 K reject is 14 W/W.  Until 0.12.5 this note said real machines run 15-25% of Carnot, which no source gives, above the best tested point, and which gives 56-93 W/W rather than the 50-150 band.  The band is an estimate.  NASA's ZBO and eCryo programmes have run 20 K coolers on the ground; nothing has flown on a propellant tank.
This is the row that turns boil-off from a fact into a CHOICE: spend array mass and power, keep the hydrogen.  Module 4 does not offer that choice yet — it applies boiloff_pct_per_day passively — so hydrolox is charged the full 0.05%/day with no option to buy it down.  That is conservative for hydrolox and it is a known gap, not a modelling decision.

name: Cryocooler specific mass (20 K)
unit: kg per W lifted at 20 K
notes:
Cold head, compressor, recuperator and radiator.  Pairs with the row above: a tank leaking 20 W needs ~100 kg of machine and ~1.6 kW of electrical power to hold it at zero boil-off, and the array for that 1.6 kW is another ~27 kg at 1 AU and ~240 kg at 3 AU.  Which is why zero-boil-off is a near-Sun answer and passive tolerance is the far one.
Source: NASA's 20 W / 20 K reverse-turbo-Brayton cooler is 5.5 kg/W on its flight-like mass projection (106.3 kg, against 336.9 kg as tested), against a project goal of 4.4 and a previous state of the art of 18.7 kg/W at 1 W of lift (Nugent, Grotenrath & Johnson 2022, NTRS 20220009350, Table 1).  5.0 sits between test and goal, and the worked example matches the test: 19.2 W lifted on 1.76 kW of input.

name: Vapour-cooled shield
unit: fraction of passive boil-off removed
notes: Route the boil-off gas through a shield on its way overboard and it intercepts heat that would have boiled more.  Free in power, cheap in mass, and it only works while something is already boiling.  Flown on ground and airborne cryogenic systems; the 0.05%/day hydrolox figure already assumes a good passive stack including this.  SCENARIO: no test gives 0.40 [0.25, 0.60].  NASA's SHIIVER tests on a 4 m tank found under 3% less boil-off at 50% fill without dome MLI and essentially none with it (NTRS 20205008233, Table 46), and NASA's 2018 roadmap put vapour cooling at TRL 5 (NTRS 20190000305, p. 5): TRL 8 rests on ground and airborne use, not flight in this role (General_Research rc-489).

name: Bulk ore restraint (bag / hopper)
unit: kg of containment per kg of ore
notes: Tankage, primary structure and cargo restraint for loose regolith.  This is the number Module 4 carries as `return_structure_frac_of_payload`, recorded here so the cargo side of storage has a citation of its own.  ENGINEERING ESTIMATE: NASA OIG IG-18-016 gives cargo capacities but no dry masses, so no registered source sets this ratio.  0.15 is aggressive and assumes dense ore in a body-mounted hopper rather than a pressurised hold.  Before v1.10.0 it was zero and the cascade happily loaded 125 t of ore into a 500 kg can.

name: Volatile cargo containment (water ice)
unit: kg of containment per kg of volatile cargo
notes:
Water sold at a depot has to still be water on arrival.  In vacuum at 1 AU, exposed ice in sunlight sits well above its sublimation threshold and is simply gone; shaded and blanketed it is stable for decades.  So the cost is a sealed, shaded hold — heavier than an ore hopper, far lighter than a cryogen tank, and no active power.  ENGINEERING ESTIMATE: no published source gives the mass fraction or the hold's stability over cruise; see the OPERATIONAL_COSTS twin.
✅  MODELLED as of Module 4 v1.14.0, through the 'Volatile cargo containment' OPERATIONAL_COSTS row — this table is not one Module 4 loads, which is why the figure sat here unread for two releases while the pipeline priced water at every in-space destination and charged nothing to keep it through a four-year cruise.  It was not a rounding term: the best cislunar missions run ~88% water by mass, so the commodity carrying the result was the one flying free.

name: Sintered / consolidated cargo
unit: Wh per kg of ore consolidated
notes: Melt or sinter the concentrate into billets and the restraint problem mostly goes away — a solid block needs mounts, not a hopper, and it cannot migrate under thrust or leak dust into mechanisms.  Trades containment mass for processing energy at a body where power is the binding constraint.  Studied for lunar regolith (microwave sintering); not demonstrated on asteroid material.  SCENARIO: no calculation or test gives 350 [150, 800] Wh/kg.  NASA's vacuum-sintering (NTRS 20230008596) and microwave-sintering (NTRS 20205010871) work on lunar simulant reports no energy per kg (General_Research rc-492).

name: Dust mitigation and seals
unit: kg per kg of mining hardware
notes: Regolith fines are the failure mode that ended Apollo's surface EVAs early and jammed InSight's mole.  In microgravity the dust does not settle at all — Hayabusa2's impactor experiment showed ejecta persisting for hours.  Labyrinth seals, electrodynamic screens and bellows on every joint. Folded into the mining-rig recurring rate in this pipeline rather than charged separately; listed so it is visible.

name: Li-ion battery (system level)
unit: Wh per kg
notes: Cells reach 250-300 Wh/kg (NASA ~265 Wh/kg: Ali et al., Frontiers in Energy Research, 2023); packaging, harness, cell balancing and thermal roughly halve it at the system level.  130 Wh/kg is an engineering analogy: five protected NASA Li-ion packs for the D-RATS spacesuit simulators measured 124-133 Wh/kg, mean 129.6 (Bennett & Baldwin 2010, NASA/TM-2010-216906, Table 5), packs rather than spacecraft batteries (General_Research rc-342).  NASA's Li-ion state of the art is 175 Wh/kg (Schmitz et al., IEEE Aerospace 2023, NTRS 20230001487, Table 3).  Already inside the 60 W/kg 'Power system specific mass' row rather than added to it — that row is explicitly PV + PMAD + battery + structure, which is why it is 60 W/kg against ROSA's ~150 W/kg at the wing.

name: Regenerative fuel cell
unit: Wh per kg
notes:
Electrolyse water in the light, run it back through a fuel cell in the dark.  Several times a battery's energy density (NASA's 1 kW lunar-polar case: 400 Wh/kg against Li-ion's 160) and it gets better the longer the dark period, because tank mass and converter mass are separate — which is the opposite of a battery.  For a mining rig on a rotating body it is the obvious architecture, and it stores the one consumable the asteroid itself supplies.  Studied by NASA for lunar night survival; not flown.
What the density leaves out: NASA's 100 W demonstration measured 47.4% round trip for the stacks alone, before balance-of-plant power (Bennett, Smith & Jakupca, NASA/TM-20205000357, Table III), against 0.90 for the battery.  At a dark fraction of 0.5 the array oversize [(1−f) + f/η]/(1−f) is 2.11× with a battery and 3.11× at 0.474, so part of the storage mass saved is paid back in array.  The 400 Wh/kg is one NASA design case: 1 kW for a 120 h lunar-polar night, 300 kg (Csank, Electric Power on the Lunar Surface, NTRS 20240013588, slide 12).  NASA puts RFC systems at ~100-600 Wh/kg with power and duration, 550 for a 350 h equatorial night and 200 for a 13 h Mars one, so the value and its range are mission-dependent estimates, not an asteroid figure (General_Research rc-414).

name: Flywheel energy storage
unit: Wh per kg
notes:
Unlimited cycle life and it doubles as a momentum wheel, which a rotating-body operation needs anyway.  NASA G2 flywheel ran on the ground at 60,000 rpm; the ISS flight unit was cancelled. Energy density is no better than lithium, so it only wins where cycle count or attitude control dominates.
ESTIMATE: the 100 Wh/kg has no source.  The G2 report (Jansen & Dever, NASA/CR-2006-213862) describes a 525 W-hr, 1 kW module built for a laboratory, where weight was not a significant factor, and gives no Wh/kg.  Comparator: NASA's G2 gives 5.3 Wh/kg usable at the module and 23.1 Wh/kg for the rotor alone, a lab demonstrator where weight did not matter; 100 and its range stay estimates without a defined mass boundary (General_Research rc-416).

name: Eclipse / night-side power fraction
unit: fraction of mission time without sunlight
notes:
A rig anchored to a rotating body is in shadow about half the time — typical asteroid rotation periods run 2-20 h, so the dark period is hours, not the 35 minutes of a LEO eclipse. Sizing storage for it roughly DOUBLES the power system for a given continuous draw.  Vesta comparator: the solar disk is "typically seen about half the time in the tropics", while annual mean visibility runs 0.363-0.566 across the body with latitude, tilt, shape and topography (Stubbs & Wang 2012, Icarus 217, p. 275).  0.50 is a scenario geometry, not a generic asteroid fraction, and no source sets the range (General_Research rc-413).
✅  MODELLED as of Module 4 v1.14.0, through the 'Eclipse / night-side dark fraction', 'Energy storage usable specific energy' and 'Power-system row baseline dark period' OPERATIONAL_COSTS rows.  Module 4 now installs [(1−f) + f/η]/(1−f) = 2.11× the continuous draw and adds the storage the body's OWN rotation period demands, less what the 60 W/kg row already carries.  Radioisotope plants are exempt and the EP array is exempt — one is flat with time, the other is in permanent sunlight.

name: RTG specific power
unit: W-electric per kg
notes: GPHS-RTG: 290 We at 56 kg = 5.2 W/kg (Cassini, New Horizons). MMRTG: 110 We at 44 kg = 2.5 W/kg (Curiosity, Perseverance) — worse, because it is designed to work in an atmosphere too. Flat with heliocentric distance, which is the entire point: at 1 AU the 60 W/kg solar row beats it twelve times over, at 3 AU solar falls to 6.7 W/kg and they cross, and past ~3.2 AU nuclear wins outright.  The pipeline's catalog runs well past 3 AU.

name: Fission surface power (Kilopower class)
unit: W-electric per kg
notes: KRUSTY (2018) was a ground nuclear test of a 5 kW(thermal) prototype for a 1 kW(electric)-class Kilopower system, on HEU U-7.65Mo fuel.  Electrical conversion was shown only in part, by two Stirling converters with dummy heat rejection for the rest (Poston et al., KRUSTY Reactor Design, Nuclear Technology 206, 2020; McClure et al., same issue), so it demonstrated the reactor, not a 1 kWe power system.  It was the first new US space reactor test in decades.  A 10 kWe unit is a design estimate, not a flown one: 1,544 kg preliminary (Gibson, Mason & Bowman 2015, NASA/TM-2015-218460, Table I; General_Research rc-349), ~1,500 kg rounded, so 6.7 W/kg, and unlike an RTG it scales: the reactor mass is dominated by shielding and radiator, not by fuel.  The only power source in this table that could run a hundred-kilowatt beneficiation plant at 3 AU.

name: Orbital propellant depot (cryogenic)
unit: % of stored mass lost per day
notes: A depot beats a spacecraft tank on boil-off for one geometric reason: heat leak scales with area and capacity with volume, so a big tank leaks proportionally less.  It can also afford the cryocooler and the sunshade that a departure stage cannot. Nothing has flown; SpaceX's propellant-transfer demonstration is the nearest thing in progress.  SCENARIO: 0.03 [0.01, 0.10] %/day has no named basis.  Modelled comparators: under 0.05%/day for a passive, shielded, ten-layer-MLI Centaur-based LEO depot (Honour et al., NTRS 20110013691); 0.5-1.0%/month of LO2 and 2.5-5.0%/month of LH2 under 60-layer MLI, varying with orbit and tank (Perrin & Casler, NTRS 20160012100, Table 11) (General_Research rc-490).

name: Depot refuelling flights to escape
unit: tanker launches per fully-fuelled departure
notes: Tanker launches to fill a Starship in LEO before a high-energy departure.  NASA OIG IG-26-004, p11, gives more than 10 after a depot launch, one every 6 days, and 12 sits inside it; the low end is Musk's eight (Aug 2021, per Wikipedia).  The high end of 16 has no source, and no SpaceX publication states a range.  Carried on the vehicle row as `tanker_flights_for_escape` and charged by Module 4 from v1.9.0.  Before that, Starship's 27 t to escape — which is larger than its GTO payload precisely BECAUSE it assumes refuelling — was priced at a single $90M launch.  The vehicle row had said so in prose since v1.4.0.  A high-energy asteroid departure scenario: NASA's OIG says lunar HLS needs at least 15 tanker Starships to a LEO depot (IG-26-010, p. 11), a different architecture (General_Research rc-355).

name: In-space propellant transfer loss
unit: fraction of transferred mass lost per transfer
notes: Chill-down of the receiving tank, residuals in the transfer line, and ullage settling.  The 1% low end is consistent with a ground LH2 transfer study (0.00-0.24 wt% with a variable-speed pump, 0.76-1.06 wt% fixed-speed; Krog & Berstad, arXiv:2512.04609, a preprint), which assumes space-rated pump hardware nobody has flown.  Cryogenic transfer in microgravity has been done at small scale (Robotic Refueling Mission, storables) and never at stage scale.  Not modelled by Module 4 — tanker flights are charged, transfer losses are not.

name: ISRU propellant depot (asteroid water)
unit: USD per kg of propellant delivered to depot
notes: The endpoint the whole pipeline points at: water mined, electrolysed or simply boiled, and left in orbit for the next vehicle.  Carried as `isru_processing_usd_per_kg` in Module 4, where it prices the ISRU return propellant a mission makes for ITSELF.  Selling propellant to a third party is a different market with a different depth, and Module 2 does not price it — the in-space demand ceilings cover materials, not fuel.
